result:
You have never seen your own face. Not once, not really. Mirrors offer only reversals; photographs capture frozen instants from the outside. What you carry in your mind as "my face" is actually a composite—fragments assembled from reflections, glimpses, other people's reactions, and pure imagination. Everyone else on Earth has seen your face more authentically than you ever will.

This strange asymmetry runs deeper still. You cannot hear your own voice the way others hear it; it reaches your ears partly through bone conduction, warmer and lower than the sound that travels to the world. You perceive yourself through instruments that distort, while everyone else receives you unfiltered.

Yet the people who love us become mirrors of a kind. They hold versions of us we can never access directly—our laugh as it sounds across a room, the expression we make while absorbed in a book, the way we look when we believe no one is watching. Somewhere in their memories exists a complete portrait of us, one we are never permitted to view.

Perhaps that's why being known feels so much like being seen. When someone says "that's so you," they are describing a person we cannot fully meet. Intimacy might simply be this: entrusting another person with the job of witnessing us, and believing—without any possible proof—that what they see is true.

We spend our lives as strangers to our own faces, and somehow that makes it bearable, even beautiful, that others are not.
